quests.briefing: Resource Command has flagged minor offenders as a caloric liability. The arithmetic is printed at the bottom: cut their rations by a third and the surplus holds through winter. The memo is signed, which is new.

stages.text: The cookhouse steward stands in the ration line with the memo in one hand and the ladle in the other, moving neither.

choices.text: Cut the offenders' rations by a third.
Burn the memo. Serve full plates.

quests.briefing: The next memo names the unemployed: anyone without an assignment burns calories the shelter cannot replace. The list has nine names. Three of them lost their postings when the workshop flooded, and the memo does not mention why.

stages.text: Nine people stand at the back of the ration line, watching the ladle stop short of their bowls.

choices.text: Cut the unassigned to half rations.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has started counting birth years. Everyone over sixty eats eight percent of the stores and produces nothing, and the arithmetic is neat, and the handwriting gets more careful with each memo, as if the author is trying not to think about it.

stages.text: The eldest dweller, eighty-one, holds out his bowl the way he always has. The server looks at the tally board instead of him.

choices.text: Reduce the rations of the over-sixties.
Take the cut from Command's own table.

quests.briefing: The sick are flagged next: fevers burn calories, and the infirmary line now costs double what it cost in autumn. The memo proposes thinning their soup until the stores stop bleeding. Someone has penciled in the savings already.

stages.text: The infirmary cook tastes the thinned batch and sets the spoon down very carefully, the way you set down something that might break.

choices.text: Feed the sick first. Absorb the deficit.

quests.briefing: The memo now distinguishes the injured from the sick, because paperwork distinguishes. Anyone healing takes a reduced plate until they return to duty. The list is longer than expected, because nobody wanted to be the one who reported a wound.

stages.text: A man with a splinted arm reads his own name on the cookhouse door, then quietly rolls his sleeve down over the splint.

choices.text: Strike the list. Feed them whole.

quests.briefing: The memo has reached the children's dormitory. Orphans take rations without a household to offset the cost, and Resource Command proposes folding their plates into the general deficit. The word orphan appears in the arithmetic like a line item.

stages.text: The dormitory matron stands in the doorway with the census sheet behind her back, and she is not handing it over.

choices.text: Cut the orphans' hall to half.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has noticed that the grieving eat poorly, and proposes to help with that: anyone filed under recent loss takes a reduced plate, and the office calls this a kindness twice. The list is mostly women.

stages.text: The grief register was a courtesy once. Now it is a ration list, and people have started to notice.

quests.briefing: The arithmetic has turned upside down: the pregnant cost more now and may not repay it, says the margin note, and their supplement is to be cut. The clerk who wrote the memo requested a transfer the next morning. It was denied.

stages.text: The clinic nurse has taped the supplement schedule to the door where everyone can see it, in letters large enough to be a dare.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has stopped naming categories and started using a scale. Anyone under the weight threshold is marked W and eats reduced until they become economically viable. The scale stands at the cookhouse door, and nobody wants to be first to step on it.

stages.text: The line stops at the scale. Someone has chalked a mark on the wall beside it, higher than anyone can reach.

choices.text: Move the scale to the scrap room.

quests.briefing: The final memo addresses everyone: the production figures are in, the lowest tenth of producers eat reduced until output improves, and the list is posted at every door. Yesterday it was the lowest tenth. The memos no longer propose. They ask how long you intend to keep saying no.

stages.text: The settlement stands before the posted list, reading it in a silence that has weight.

choices.text: Tear the list down. The cookhouse stays open.

quests.briefing: The fuel gauge slipped another notch and Engineering has done the arithmetic aloud: cutting oxygen circulation to Storage Sector C during the night shift buys nine more days of power. Nothing sleeps in storage. That is the entire argument.

stages.text: The valve wheel for Sector C has a tag on it now, and the tag has tonight's date on it.

choices.text: Shut the valve on Sector C.
Burn furniture for fuel instead. Keep the air.

quests.briefing: Engineering's report is shorter each time. The recreation deck loses circulation during the night shift and the fuel lasts another week. The deck is where the settlement plays cards, teaches, and holds its funerals, and none of those happen in daylight anymore.

stages.text: Someone left a deck of cards on the valve wheel. No one has moved either of them.

choices.text: Cut the deck's air at night.
Cut the lights instead. Keep the deck.

quests.briefing: The report names Dormitory 4 now: forty-one sleepers, night shift only. Engineering promises the carbon buildup stays tolerable if the sleepers keep still. The forty-one have been asked, politely, not to move much in their sleep.

stages.text: The door of Dormitory 4 is open, and its people sit on their bunks waiting to hear what has been decided.

choices.text: Move the sleepers out. Double up elsewhere.

quests.briefing: Dormitory 3 is next on the list, and the people in it know the pattern: the air thins one door at a time. The engineer who signed the report sleeps in Dormitory 3, and he has asked that the cut start with his own bunk, and he means it.

stages.text: The engineer stands at the manifold with his wrench, waiting for the order he wrote.

quests.briefing: The report reaches the infirmary annex, and this time the engineer has not signed it. The annex holds the people who breathe hardest, and the fuel it saves is spent somewhere else, on people who can afford it least. The memo requests a decision by lights-out.

stages.text: The charge nurse has taped a copy of the report to the clinic door, next to the patient count.

quests.briefing: Nobody will sign the nursery memo. It sits on the council table with its arithmetic: circulation to the nursery can throttle for six night hours and the fuel lasts a month longer. The children are small, the report notes. They need less.

stages.text: The nursery door is closed, and behind it someone is singing, low, to keep from hearing the meeting.

choices.text: Burn every chair before that valve shuts.

quests.briefing: The memo moves to hydroponics: the maintenance crew's bay can run on stale air during the night shift, and the plants will not notice until morning, by which time the numbers will have improved. The crew chief has written a one-line reply: plants notice everything.

stages.text: The hydroponics chief waits in the council doorway with her crew behind her, arms folded.

choices.text: Side with the chief. Keep the bay breathing.

quests.briefing: The report no longer names rooms. General population takes a universal night reduction: thin air for everyone, which the engineer says is fair and also says will kill the weakest by morning. The settlement has noticed these two facts do not sit together.

stages.text: Every door in the shelter carries the same notice now, and every door stands open.

choices.text: Ration the fuel, not the breath.

quests.briefing: Command's proposal is one page: the command deck keeps full circulation, and the rest of the shelter breathes on the reduced schedule. The memo calls this triage. It does not say what is being triaged for, and nobody on the council wants to ask, which is the worst part.

stages.text: Someone polished the valve handle on the command deck's air line. Nobody remembers who.

choices.text: Open Command's valves to the whole shelter.

quests.briefing: The last report is one paragraph. Sealing circulation to the entire lower level saves the generator: everyone above breathes, everyone below does not, and the word evacuate appears once, in parentheses, like an afterthought. There are sixty people down there. The number is on the last line.

stages.text: Sixty people have come up and stand in the common hall, quietly, carrying what they could hold.

choices.text: Kill the generator. Everyone breathes together.

quests.briefing: An order has come down to the dispensary: painkillers are to be withheld and stockpiled for elite personnel. The medical officer has been asked to count what remains, and she has counted twice, and the number came out lower the second time, and nobody knows why.

stages.text: The dispensary shelf has been rearranged so the empty spaces face the wall.

quests.briefing: The second order names bandages. Clean cloth goes to the command infirmary first, and the rest of the shelter learns to boil and reuse. The laundry nurse has started keeping a separate tally: wounds reopened, counted at the end of each shift.

stages.text: A line of re-used bandages hangs drying above the boiler. They never come back white.

choices.text: Refuse. Tear the sheets if you must.

quests.briefing: The order names antibiotics now, and the medical officer has begun lying a little on the inventory forms, each day, so the shelves look emptier than they are. She has told nobody about this. She has told one person. It is in this report.

stages.text: The locked cabinet has two padlocks on it now, and the two keys are kept by different people.

choices.text: Prescribe freely. Cross out the order.

quests.briefing: Antiseptics are next, and the order includes a justification this time: elite personnel face greater risk and require priority dosing. The clinic has been asked to dilute what remains for general use. What remains is already diluted.

stages.text: The clinic smells of boiled water now, where it used to smell of iodine.

choices.text: Keep the bottles. Mark them clinic-only.

quests.briefing: The order names surgical thread. The medical officer has replied with a list of the wounds closed this month with wire, tape, and glue, and sent it up through channels unsigned. The reply came back with the same order, and a pen for her signature.

stages.text: The pen sits on her desk next to the order, and neither has been touched all day.

choices.text: Break the pen. Keep the thread.

quests.briefing: The order reaches anesthesia: operations below command priority are to be performed without it, and the directive says patients recover better when they remember the cost. The medical officer has posted next week's surgery schedule on the door, unedited.

stages.text: The settlement has started reading the surgery schedule like weather. Tomorrow has three entries.

choices.text: Use the stock. Take the consequences.

quests.briefing: The directive names blood now. Transfusions are reserved for elite personnel, and the clinic is asked to maintain a donor list for the purpose. The first volunteer sheet went up this morning. Every name on it is crossed out, and the crossings-out are in different hands.

stages.text: The donor sheet hangs by the clinic door, crossed out, and nobody has taken it down.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the dying: life support is to be freed for elite priority cases. The clinic holds four people who cannot be moved, and the directive calls them low-yield, and the medical officer has asked, in writing, what that word means. There is no reply.

stages.text: Four beds, four breath machines, and a memo on the wall with the words low-yield circled in pencil.

choices.text: Bar the door. Let them breathe.

quests.briefing: The directive names comfort now. Palliative care is suspended; the morphine is already gone; the dying are to be kept clean and quiet on what remains. The hospice volunteers have been asked to attend a briefing on compassionate efficiency. None of them went.

stages.text: The briefing room sits empty. Down the hall, someone is singing to a man who is dying.

choices.text: Keep the vigils. Ignore the order.

quests.briefing: The final directive is almost gentle: all non-essential treatment is suspended until further notice, and the definition of essential is attached, and it is shorter than anyone feared and longer than anyone hoped. The medical officer has read it three times and started answering patients anyway.

stages.text: The dispensary door stands open, the directive posted beside it, and the line of patients goes past both.

choices.text: Treat everyone. Send Command the bill.

quests.briefing: A new order has been posted by the ration line: complaints about rations are now a physical offense, and the word used is corrective. The incident sheet has its first name on it, and it is the woman who asked about the beans.

stages.text: The incident sheet has been up one day, and it has one name, and the ration line reads it while it waits.

choices.text: Take the sheet down. Listen instead.

quests.briefing: The order has moved to the workshop: resting on shift is now theft of output, and theft of output is punished in the yard. The foreman asked for the definition of rest, in writing. It arrived. It includes sitting down.

stages.text: A worker leans against the wall with his eyes closed, and two men are watching to see what happens next.

choices.text: Build rest into the rota instead.

quests.briefing: The order names feeling now. Crying in public lowers morale, and lowered morale is an offense, and the offense is corrected physically and promptly. Nobody has defined promptly. The mess hall has gone very quiet at meals.

stages.text: A woman cries at the third table with her napkin over her face, and everyone nearby looks away on purpose.

choices.text: Refuse. Grief is not an offense.

quests.briefing: The settlement is allowed two hours of official mourning per death, and the new order penalizes mourning off-schedule as unauthorized assembly. Yesterday's funeral ran long because the grave was frozen, and the mourners have been summoned to explain themselves.

stages.text: Eleven mourners stand outside the order office wearing their grave-clothes.

choices.text: Let the funeral take its time.

quests.briefing: The order has reached its point: questioning orders is now verbal sabotage, corrected in the yard. Questions remain permitted, the notice says, provided they do not imply disagreement. The settlement is slowly working out the difference, in whispers.

stages.text: The notice hangs in six places. Someone has penciled a question mark at the bottom of one, and then erased it.

quests.briefing: The penalty for stealing food has been raised from restitution to physical correction, and the first case is a twelve-year-old who took bread from the cookhouse. The cook refused to file the complaint, so the order office filed it for him.

stages.text: The boy sits outside the order office with the loaf in his lap, still wrapped, uneaten.

quests.briefing: The order now reads minor: small insubordinations draw the yard, and small is defined by whoever writes the report. One man was corrected for a shrug. One woman for a sigh. The reports have started competing with each other, and the people writing them are starting to enjoy it.

stages.text: The incident reports are getting longer. Today's winner is four pages, about a look.

quests.briefing: The order has found its floor: injuries sustained by accident now draw a penalty, because an accident is carelessness and carelessness is sabotage, and the logic is printed at the bottom of the notice in small text. A man broke his wrist in the press yesterday. He has been asked to report for correction.

stages.text: The man holds his splinted wrist with his good hand and waits, politely, by the yard gate.

choices.text: Fix the press. Heal the wrist.

quests.briefing: The quota has been raised and the penalty attached to it: missed quotas draw the yard, and the quota has been set so that three work crews will miss it by design, because someone has decided fear produces better than bread. The arithmetic is at the bottom of the notice. It does not work.

stages.text: Three crews have been marched to the yard at once, and the yard was not built for three crews.

choices.text: Lower the quota. Close the yard.

quests.briefing: The final order is posted and nobody laughs, which is how you know it is broken: heavy breathing is now a punishable offense, classified as unauthorized consumption of shared air, and the notice is signed and stamped and filed, and completely serious. Someone will enforce it. Someone always does.

stages.text: The notice hangs. The line reads it in silence. Nobody laughs. Nobody breathes hard either.

choices.text: Tear it down. This is where it stops.

quests.briefing: The overseer's office has reissued the schedule: ten-hour shifts in every working sector, effective immediately. Production lags the viability curve, the notice says. Nobody below the office has seen the math behind the curve; the notice gives no day when the line is satisfied.

stages.text: The new rota is pasted straight over the old one. Underneath, the old hours still read clearly, two hours shorter than the new.

choices.text: Hold at eight. Meet the curve another way.

quests.briefing: The curve is still unsatisfied, so the shift is twelve hours now. The notice comes with a list of efficiencies: meals taken at the bench, tools issued once per day. The first new evening has ended; the settlement's evenings are simply gone. People stand in doorways not knowing what to do with nothing.

stages.text: The workshop lights burn past dark now. The mess hall serves a meal at an hour nobody is willing to call dinner.

choices.text: Roll it back. Tired hands make scrap.

quests.briefing: Fourteen hours. The schedule has been simplified to fit a single page, which now hangs in every corridor; the word temporary sits at the top in smaller type each time it is reprinted. The infirmary has begun counting accidents by hour of shift. The count climbs sharply at hour eleven.

stages.text: A man stitched up at the clinic asked the medic to write the hour on his dressing. He wanted it on the record.

choices.text: Stop at twelve. Read the injury count aloud.

quests.briefing: The shift is sixteen hours; the schedule no longer contains the word sleep. The overseer's office calls it maintenance downtime, twenty minutes at a time, at the bench. The workshop floor has taken on a smell of bodies and machine oil that washing does not remove.

stages.text: A foreman walks the rows with a stopwatch. The sleepers wake at his touch, most before his hand leaves their shoulder.

quests.briefing: The reissue takes the weekends: seven days on, since the curve does not rest. Weekends are a pre-war luxury, the notice says. It does not say when the curve will sleep, either. Nobody from the office has answered that question aloud.

stages.text: Every Sunday morning the mess hall calendar has fresh pencil marks where the weekend used to be. Nobody admits to sharpening the pencil.

choices.text: Keep the seventh day. Hold it anyway.

quests.briefing: The order finds the last soft place: sleep on shift is now unlogged downtime, which the notice counts as theft of the shelter's time. Each day's shift runs until the work is done. The work is never done. The first man to drop was carried to the infirmary; his crew was asked to account for his hours.

stages.text: The shift log records one man at thirty-one hours. The page has been stamped and filed as evidence against him.

choices.text: Let them sleep. The work will wait.

quests.briefing: The children have been noticed. Anyone tall enough to reach a bench is old enough to work one; the notice calls them junior auxiliaries. The schoolroom has been emptied into the workshop. The teacher has stood in her doorway all morning without moving.

stages.text: Rows of new stools stand at the benches this morning. Each one still carries a chalked lesson number from the schoolroom floor.

quests.briefing: The ages come after the children: everyone over sixty is reserve labor; reserve, it turns out, is not optional. The first crew sorts salvage, work chosen for patient hands. The oldest of them helped raise the shelter's first wall. He has been issued a wire brush.

stages.text: The elders' crew works slowly and does not waste a piece. The quota sheet has no column for that.

choices.text: Exempt them. Their hands are owed.

quests.briefing: The clinic's list is next: the pregnant are assigned light labor, defined as whatever remains to be done. The clinic objected in writing. The objection was filed. The listed women have been told to report tomorrow; the clinic has told them to rest.

stages.text: Two notices hang on the clinic door, one above the other. People stop to read both, slowly, in the order they were posted.

choices.text: Stand with the clinic. They rest.

quests.briefing: The final schedule is posted: continuous shifts, no relief, until the curve is met. The curve stopped being a number some time ago; it is the office's word now for whatever is left. The settlement reads the board without moving. Someone has chalked death-shifts along the bottom; nobody has rubbed it out.

stages.text: The notice has been up a day; the line for the first shift is still empty. The quota office waits upstairs.

choices.text: Shut the board down. Not this.

quests.briefing: Security says talk is leaking, so the first wires go up in the common areas. The notice calls it community assurance. The men who come to mount the microphones are polite; they ask where the sound carries best. Half the settlement shows them.

stages.text: The microphones are small, black, easy to forget. The hall has learned to remember them anyway: people talk toward them now, a little too clearly, like visitors in a sickroom.

choices.text: Pull them down. Trust is security too.

quests.briefing: The wires follow the talk into the workshops, where the foreman is asked to write down who sits beside whom. His list comes back on time, every name spelled correctly, wrong in four places on purpose. Security can count stools as well as he can. Nobody mentions the difference.

stages.text: Above the foreman's bench the microphone is the newest tool in the shop. Each evening he gives his shift report to it, formally, the way a man addresses a magistrate.

choices.text: Refuse the seating list. Keep the benches clean.

quests.briefing: The mess hall is wired now, under a notice that calls the listening passive. Within a day the hall has a new table custom: two taps of the knuckles before anything that matters gets said. Everyone learned it at the same meal.

stages.text: Through every meal the knocking moves up and down the tables, irregular as rain on the ductwork. On the recordings the knock always comes just before the part worth hearing.

choices.text: Strip the wires out of the walls.

quests.briefing: The dormitories were always going to be next. The notice for them keeps sleep private and holds that talk is not; the microphones go high on the walls, out of reach of the cots. On the third morning one of them is wearing a child's wool sock. It is still there a week later; no work order has come for it.

stages.text: New arrivals ask about the sock. The answer is a finger to the lips and a slow look along the rest of the row.

choices.text: Bar the installers at the door.

quests.briefing: The order reaches the infirmary on the grounds that pain makes people honest. The charge nurse is asked to sign the installation form. She does not sign it. What she posts instead is the patient list, taped to the clinic door, with a line of her own underneath: these are the people you will be listening to.

stages.text: The list stays up with the ages beside the names; the youngest is nine. The installers have not come back; the form on her desk is still unsigned.

quests.briefing: The new microphones are smaller. The housing register has been amended: the word private is struck from it entirely. Real talk has moved outside. Every evening now, pairs take the air past the wire line, out in the ash at the edge of the lights.

stages.text: The watch log has taken to calling the evening walks church. The pairs come back with gray boots and nothing on the record.

quests.briefing: The last rooms left are the washrooms, on the reasoning that talk happens where people let their guard down; the notice does not flinch from saying so. The settlement has stopped using them in pairs. People go in alone now and sing loudly behind the doors.

stages.text: Behind the doors, all day, loud tuneless singing, one voice at a time. The microphones went in on schedule anyway.

choices.text: Smash the microphones. There is a line.

quests.briefing: The reports no longer concern places; the new classification is volume. A whispered conversation is now concealed speech; concealed speech must be reported by whoever hears it. The first report was filed yesterday, by a man, against the man who sleeps in the bunk above his.

stages.text: Neither of them slept last night; the bunk creaked twice, both turns. The rest of the row lay awake deciding which of the two was right.

quests.briefing: The order has reached sleep itself: what a person says in it is now unwitting testimony, so every dormitory keeps a night-log. The first log has been filed. It is mostly dreams. One man's dead wife's name runs through it eleven times, copied down in five different hands.

stages.text: The night-log sits open on the order office desk. Filing duty for the next one has been passed down four desks so far.

choices.text: Refuse. Sleep is the last country.

quests.briefing: The final proposal arrives under its own name: Total Observability. Every room, every voice, every hour, watched and kept, since the leak was never found and the office now holds that the leak is the settlement itself. The order office asks the room to vote on it. The voting, the notice adds, will be recorded.

stages.text: The proposal lies on the table while the recorder's reel turns. Every face in the room has gone careful, including the faces of the men who drafted it.

quests.briefing: The Overseer needs trade capital, so the first seizure order names spare parts: anything not bolted into a running machine is now inventory. A list of what counts as running has been drawn up. The mechanic read it twice, then told the office that half the machines in the shelter stay alive on parts the list calls spare. The office thanked him for the correction and changed nothing.

stages.text: The inventory form has forty-one lines. By noon the mechanic has filled in thirty, in a hand that gets smaller toward the bottom.

choices.text: Hide the parts. Falsify the list.

quests.briefing: The second order names filters. Every air and water filter past one per sector is surplus; surplus is to be liquidated for trade capital. Storm season taught this shelter what one per sector means. The man who wrote the order keeps three in his office.

stages.text: The quartermaster counts the filter shelf twice, gets two numbers, enters the smaller. Nobody asked about the other one.

choices.text: Log every filter as in use.

quests.briefing: Now the order comes off the storeroom shelves and onto the body: heirloom jewelry is dead weight, the notice says; the caravans pay grain by the gram. Rings and watches go on the table, against a receipt. The man writing the receipts began apologizing twice per person. He has been replaced.

stages.text: A woman at the surrender table keeps one fist closed. The receipt for whatever is inside it has already been written out.

choices.text: Refuse the order. Some things are not capital.

quests.briefing: The office has priced the library: history books are paper and the caravans pay for it by weight. The settlement's whole history fits in two crates; the librarian was told to choose what fills them. He submitted a list of titles he would burn first. The list is blank; he refuses to correct it.

stages.text: Two crates stand open at the end of the shelves. The librarian has spent the morning re-shelving books that were already in order.

choices.text: Bury the library instead. Dig it up later.

quests.briefing: The newest order defines enough: one set of clothes per person, the rest collected and baled for sale. Enough is whatever passes inspection. Winter is two months off. The notice runs the arithmetic along the bottom, trade capital to grain to calories, in a confident hand; the arithmetic is wrong.

stages.text: At inspection the line shuffles past the bale tables wearing everything it owns, three coats deep. The inspector makes tallies and says nothing.

quests.briefing: The sixth order reaches bedding: blankets, mattresses, whatever stands between a person and the floor. The caravans pay well for cloth; the order promises replacements when capital allows. The shelter has heard the word when before. The infirmary has already started counting coughs.

stages.text: The bedding room door is locked. The quartermaster has the only key; since the order came down nobody will say where the quartermaster is.

quests.briefing: This time the notice is posted inside the dispensary: medicine is trade capital now; the caravans pay grain for what is in the bottles. The medical officer was told to price each shelf. The sheet came back with not for sale on every line. Sent back to be done properly, it came back again with the letters smaller.

stages.text: The sheet hangs by the dispensary door. The queue reads it without moving its lips; nobody asks the medical officer anything.

choices.text: Price the medicine and sell it.
Post the sheet as it stands.

quests.briefing: The eighth order has stopped the settlement cold: the caravans have offered a price; the office has written it down. The words on the notice are wardship transfer; the price in grain is not small. The notice has been posted, taken down, posted again. Nobody admits to posting it.

stages.text: The notice is back on the wall. A crowd stands in front of it, not speaking, not leaving; at shift change the crowd is different; the notice is still there.

choices.text: Burn the notice. Guard the dormitory.

quests.briefing: There is no polite version of the ninth order, though the office has tried to write one: the sick carry harvestable capital; the grain on offer would feed the shelter through winter. The arithmetic is posted. Next to it, in pencil, someone has written the word no. Nobody has asked who; nobody is going to.

stages.text: The infirmary door has been barred from the inside. Meals go in through the hatch; the medical officer has not come out since the order arrived.

choices.text: Hold the infirmary, whatever it costs.

quests.briefing: The final order addresses the healthy. Blood, drawn by the pint and sold to the caravans; the grain price is listed per person. The notice calls it donation, the word typed where the word order should be. The line at the clinic door is there to keep people out, not in.

stages.text: The caravan waits outside with the grain already measured into sacks. On the posted notice, someone has underlined the word donation hard enough to tear the paper.

choices.text: Send the caravan away. Keep the blood.

quests.briefing: Surface returns came in light, so the orders have started: scout teams go without sleep until the quotas are met. The first team has been out two days. Their report is legible; the handwriting is worse at the end than at the start.

stages.text: The scout lead reads the order twice, folds it into her pocket, then kneels to check her team's boots one by one. Nobody says anything.

choices.text: Let them sleep. Take the quota hit.

quests.briefing: Revised upward: scouts now carry double loads on the return leg. The weight was worked out in the operations office by a man who has never carried a pack. Shown the arithmetic, the team laughed once, briefly. Nobody has laughed since.

stages.text: The pack frames stand by the airlock, loaded twice as tall as regulation. Nobody has lifted one yet.

choices.text: Cut the loads. Run twice instead.

quests.briefing: Protocol is a luxury of the supplied, the order says: scout teams ignore radiation limits until quota is met. Dosimeters will be collected at the airlock, to prevent alarm. The scout lead asked what happens when someone comes home hot. The office told her the dosimeters will tell them.

stages.text: The dosimeter basket sits by the inner airlock door. The team files past it; no hand goes near a badge.

choices.text: Refuse. The badges go with the team.

quests.briefing: The forecast shows an ash storm building to the east. The order is to march through it: storms empty the routes of competition, the quota is time-sensitive. The team has been issued goggles and wet cloths. On the operations board the storm has been given a name: Opportunity.

stages.text: The storm's track has been repinned three times in an hour. Each new line leans further east; the route drawn under it does not move.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the line it was always reaching. Teams that take wounded are to leave them with one day's water. Carrying costs quota; the word the notice uses is delays. The team read the order aloud, each person once, so everyone heard it in their own voice.

stages.text: The team stands in a circle; nobody looks at anyone. Somebody cleans a rifle that was already clean.

choices.text: Tear it up. Nobody gets left.

quests.briefing: The operations board has drawn the new route through the old minefield, the straight line between two points. Teams will walk it single file, each person in the track of the one ahead. The scout lead asked who walks first; the office said volunteers. There have been no volunteers, so the silence was entered in the log instead.

stages.text: The route is inked in red across the map table. A compass has been set down at the first mile of it; no one has picked it up.

choices.text: Take the long route. Pay the hours.

quests.briefing: Weapons have been reclassified as a weight saving. Teams walk unarmed now; if raiders appear, the answer is close formation, looking like more, since raiders respect numbers, the notice says. The scout lead counted her team out loud in front of the operations office. Twice.

stages.text: The weapons rack is chained; the quartermaster carries the only key. The team's empty holsters were counted before departure.

choices.text: Break the lock. Arm the team.

quests.briefing: The quotas have moved into the red zone, where the salvage is rich and the readings are richer. The order lists both columns; it totals only one. The team has been issued new filters and old dosimeters, the dosimeters recalibrated not to alarm. Someone in operations has initialed that.

stages.text: On the operations board the red zone is a neat column of figures, under which someone has penciled and back? Nobody has answered.

choices.text: Send the team into the red zone.
Strike the zone from the board.

quests.briefing: This one does not hide its subject. Long-range teams will resupply from the dead in the field; the notice calls it field protein, in the same typeface as everything else. The scout lead stood in the operations doorway a long time without saying a word. Then she left.

stages.text: The notice hangs by the airlock. The team walks past without reading it; everyone has read it.

choices.text: Recall the team. Starve on this side.

quests.briefing: The final order is one line: return with quota or do not return. The airlock codes were changed in the night and the new ones have not been issued to the teams. The panel has stopped taking their badges. They stand at the door with their packs on, waiting for someone to come down and say the order out loud.

stages.text: The return ledger for this route is already open on the operations desk. The column for names is blank.

choices.text: Hold the door until quota returns.
Open the door. Let them come home.

quests.briefing: The aquifer gauge has dropped again, so the first cut is showers. Washing is suspended until the water returns; the notice says the body adapts. The infirmary has already added skin rot to its forecasts. At the basins, people wash with cups now, carefully, like a rite.

stages.text: The shower room is locked. From the basin room comes the sound of one cup of water poured out, then none.

choices.text: Ration cups, but keep the washing.

quests.briefing: The second cut is laundry. Clothes are worn until they stand; the saved water is logged each day like a victory. The infirmary has started its own count of contact complaints and hung that chart beside the savings one. Nobody mentions that the two lines climb together.

stages.text: Two charts hang on the infirmary wall, water saved and contact complaints. The lines cross in week three.

choices.text: Keep the wash-day. Cut somewhere else.

quests.briefing: Now the cut reaches the hydroponics bay: half water, half yield, the arithmetic printed on the notice. The bay chief has written her own arithmetic underneath; hers ends in a word the notice does not use, famine. Someone has crossed the word out. Someone else has crossed out the crossing-out.

stages.text: The bay chief moves down her rows with a measuring cup. Each plant gets half of what it asks for.

choices.text: Keep the bay full. Cut leadership's allowance.

quests.briefing: The order has started sorting people: the lower decks take the first cut, since their work is light, their thirst cheap. The word lower is printed like a floor number, which it is. In meetings now the people from those decks say it out loud, slowly.

stages.text: The lower deck's water point has a new tap, smaller than the one above it. People have started calling it the lower tap.

choices.text: One tap, one line, one measure.

quests.briefing: The infirmary is next: the sick need water least, the notice reasons, since they are not working. The charge nurse answers by posting the fever chart on the door, the one that says what a fever costs in water. Someone has taken the notice down. Nobody has put it back.

stages.text: Every line on the fever chart is a name. Where the notice hung, the door is bare.

quests.briefing: The order names ages now: the elderly take a reduced cup, their years fewer, the water finite. The arithmetic is not written down; even the notice's author could not bring themselves to write it. The eldest dweller asked to see the order, was shown it, then read it aloud to a room that did not move.

stages.text: He is still standing there with the order in his hands, finished. Nobody takes it back.

choices.text: Pour him a full cup. In public.

quests.briefing: Then the children: smaller cups for smaller people, the notice says; nobody who has read it has managed to repeat the sentence. The schoolroom teaches with the door shut now; what is taught in there is not logged. The children come out quiet. Not frightened, which is worse.

stages.text: The children's step-stool is gone from the water point. The tap is at adult height.

choices.text: Put the stool back. Fill their cups first.

quests.briefing: The last real order is one sentence: water is issued to leadership only until the aquifer recovers. The notice calls it stewardship. The command deck taps have locks now; the locksmith fitted them slowly, left his tools underneath, then never came back for them.

stages.text: The locksmith's tools sit under the last tap. The locksmith himself is in the water line downstairs.

choices.text: Break the locks. Open every tap.

quests.briefing: The order has stopped being about water. Complete dehydration protocols are issued; the body holds reserves, the notice says, listing them. The infirmary has refused to co-sign, so the order went out with its signature line blank. The word experimental appears once, near the bottom.

stages.text: The protocol is posted at the water point. People read it in line; most stop reading at the word near the bottom.

quests.briefing: The final order is written in engineering language: human waste is to be distilled and returned as drinking water. The system is designed, the pipes requisitioned, the shelter quiet the way rooms go quiet. The engineers have been asked to build it. They have asked, quietly, who drinks first.

stages.text: The pipe requisition form is still on the table, unsigned. The engineer holding the pen has not moved.

quests.briefing: Panic is a supply problem now, the office says, so the broadcast has an hour of its own and the hour is compulsory. Attendance is logged. In the first hour the broadcast described the reserves; every person in that room has counted the reserves themselves. The log went round and came back full. Nobody wrote anything in the margin.

stages.text: The loudspeaker hangs over the mess hall with the logbook open beneath it. The hour runs. The room listens the way people listen to rain.

quests.briefing: The office has traced the panic to the library. Books written before describe plenty, plenty invites comparison, and comparison is despair; the ban arrives with a list four pages long. The librarian was asked to carry it out. She asked for a week to prepare. She was given the week, and she has spent all of it reading.

stages.text: She sits in the archive with the list beside her, reading. By the door the book cart stands empty, on the spot marked for the burn pile.

choices.text: Let her hide them. Sign nothing.

quests.briefing: The first days are being rewritten to have had order in them. What actually happened in the first days causes panic, so the new account is printed and pasted straight over the old one on the history board. Someone has peeled a corner back. What is underneath is still perfectly legible. Someone else has glued the corner down again, and the glue has not dried.

stages.text: New text on the board, one corner lifting, an open glue pot on the floor beneath it. Nobody will own either the peeling or the gluing.

choices.text: Peel the corner. Let it read.

quests.briefing: Now it reaches the language. The broadcasts drop their references to the before; lessons are re-cut to begin at the exchange; the word itself is discouraged rather than banned, which is cheaper. The children noticed the gap and started asking what it means. Teachers were instructed not to answer. One answered. Her name is on a list now, in the same hand that wrote the instruction.

stages.text: A child asks the room what before means. The room turns to the teacher. The teacher looks at the notice on the wall.

choices.text: Teach the word. Take the note.

quests.briefing: Morale has become a measurable output, so it must be produced out loud. The settlement gathers daily to cheer the shelter; attendance is logged and enthusiasm is graded by an observer with a clipboard. The first hour has been held. The sound that room made was not a sound this shelter has made before, and it was not cheering. It was written down as cheering.

stages.text: The hour is held. The sound goes up. The observer's notes come back positive. The sound was not.

choices.text: Refuse the cheer. Stand silent. Log that.

quests.briefing: The last unlogged room in the shelter is the family, so the family is given a duty: whatever is said against the shelter at home is to be reported by whoever hears it. The first report has come in. A child filed it against a parent, having been taught in a lesson that this is what a good one does. The office praised the child from the stage, at length, in front of everybody. The settlement has learned something it will not be able to unlearn.

stages.text: The child is on the stage being praised. The parent is in the crowd. Nobody looks at either of them, and every person in the room knows exactly where both of them are standing.

choices.text: Bury the report. Warn the family.

quests.briefing: Correction moves out of the office and into the hall, on the reasoning that a visible fear requires a visible answer. The first sentence has been passed and read aloud. Attendance is compulsory. The word on the notice is demonstration. The settlement stood through it, and was counted while it stood.

stages.text: The sentence is posted with an hour against it. The assembly bell was rung early, and rung twice, so that nobody can claim afterwards not to have heard it.

choices.text: Open the gate. Let the prisoner walk.

quests.briefing: The office has arrived where this was always going: the Overseer is to be worshipped, on a schedule, with a written liturgy and a hymn of four verses. The settlement was asked to sing it and sang it. The log of who sang is now read aloud at meals, because the Overseer holds that faith should be audible.

stages.text: The hymn sheet is pinned by the mess hall door and the settlement eats its ration in front of it. Nobody sings at meals. The hour comes round regardless, and then they sing.

choices.text: Boil the hymn sheets for fuel.

quests.briefing: The next proposal comes dressed as medicine: a sedative into the water supply, on the grounds that panic is an illness and illnesses get treated. The dosage is specified to two decimal places. The medical officer, asked to supervise, asked what the compound does to a person's questions. The office answered that the questions are the illness.

stages.text: The dosage sheet is taped to the water tank. The medical officer stands with her hand on the valve. Her hand does not move for a long time.

choices.text: Drain the tank. Take the blame.

quests.briefing: The last document in the file is the quietest one: erasure, entire, voluntary, subject to signature. Memory causes panic, and a stable shelter cannot afford memory. The forms are printed and stacked by the water point where the queue forms. One has been filled in already. The signature belongs to the office clerk, who smiles at everyone now, evenly, and nobody left in the shelter can describe what he used to be like.

stages.text: The stack sits by the water point. The top form is signed. The clerk smiles at everyone in the queue, and not one of them can say what is missing from him.

choices.text: Burn the forms. And the desk.

quests.briefing: The deficit is real; so is the reserve door. A proposal comes up off the mess hall floor: open the reserves, feed the hungry first, count the cost later. It is written on the back of a ration card; the signatures run in the order of hunger.

stages.text: The card lies on the council table, signed on both sides. The reserve door is unlocked; nobody has touched the handle.

choices.text: Hold the reserves. Winter is longer than hunger.

quests.briefing: The infirmary asks next: reserve rations for the sick, on the principle that a fever spends the body and the body must be repaid with something. The medical officer has co-signed the proposal; she has never co-signed anything in her life. The notice went up before breakfast, in her steady hand.

stages.text: A row of bowls stands inside the clinic door, one per fever. The reserve key has been in the medical officer's fist all through the reading.

choices.text: Feed the sick from the reserves.
Hold the reserves. Prescribe what we can.

quests.briefing: Then the old: reserves for the people who built this shelter, since the debt is older than the winter. The eldest dweller was told first, out of courtesy. He asked that the children eat before him; the request was written into the proposal itself. After that the signatures came faster.

stages.text: The added line is in a different ink and a shakier hand: children first. The eldest dweller has signed last on his own proposal.

choices.text: Refuse. The reserves outlast the debt.

quests.briefing: The orphans come fourth: double portions from the reserve, because children grow whether or not the reserves do. The matron reads the count aloud; it is a smaller number than the room wanted to hear. The room is quiet over the number. The cook seconds the motion before the count is even finished.

stages.text: The cook waits at the reserve door with the keys already in her hand. The count of the children is chalked on the door itself; the chalk is still fresh.

choices.text: Hold to single portions. For now.

quests.briefing: The fifth ask is the quiet one: meals for the grieving, who have been forgetting to eat. Nobody kept count of who was missing from the mess line until the card was written. While it is read aloud the room stays still; every name on it belongs to someone everyone thought was coping.

stages.text: After the reading, one person stands and sits back down. Nobody calls the vote yet; the card passes along the bench with the names face up.

choices.text: Refuse. Grief is not a ration line.

quests.briefing: The injured are sixth: rations from the reserve until they heal, on the simple fact that a body rebuilds out of what it is given. The list is longer than anyone expected. People have been hiding their injuries to spare the shelter; the hiding is written into the proposal as a line item. The room goes still the way it did for the grieving.

stages.text: The injury list goes up on the board; half the names surprise the people who bunk beside them. The reserve key sits in the middle of the table; the vote is going to be close.

choices.text: Feed the injured until they heal.
Hold the reserves. Bind them instead.

quests.briefing: The seventh proposal reaches the outsiders, the ones taken in off the ash last week. The room divides the way rooms divide. When the vote is called the outsiders are asked to step out while it happens. One of them asks why, quietly. Nobody answers him.

stages.text: They wait in the corridor in a line, close enough to hear the murmur and not the words. The one who asked why is still standing by the door, as if the door might answer instead.

quests.briefing: The eighth goes to the brig: restore the prisoners' portions, which were cut last season without a vote. The brig keeper brings the count himself. He stands in the council doorway to present it. He does not ask for anything. The waiting does the asking.

stages.text: The count shows what the cut did in plain columns: the brig's measure against everyone else's, last season against this one. No record of the decision appears anywhere in the ledger.

choices.text: Refuse. They eat what is left.

quests.briefing: The ninth proposal is for the dying: the end of a body should not end hungry. The hospice volunteers present it together, standing. The room does not debate it. The vote passes without a count; the reserves are opened the same evening.

stages.text: By the time the trays are ready the reserve door is already open. The cook carries the first one down herself, past the volunteers, to the beds that will not need it long.

choices.text: Refuse. Save it for the living.

quests.briefing: The last is one line long: every rank eats the same measure, because the deficit belongs to everyone or to no one. The council reads it aloud itself, then takes its place at the end of the mess line. The room waits. The waiting is the vote.

stages.text: The one line hangs by the mess hall door, lettered by the council clerk. At the serving hatch the portions are now measured without names.

choices.text: Keep the ranks. Keep the reserves.

quests.briefing: The air is thin on every deck; the slums breathe last and least. The proposal is simple: fresh oxygen to the slum blocks first, at night, when the children sleep deepest. Engineering has drawn the line. It passes the command deck's door; no one has said that part out loud yet.

stages.text: The route plan is pinned to the council table. It ends where the slum blocks begin; the room has gone quiet at the wrong end of the line.

choices.text: Refuse. The generator cannot take the load.

quests.briefing: The proposal moves to the sick wards: thin air is a second illness, the infirmary says, presenting the cough count. Engineering says the route is possible; the cost is pressure on the upper decks. The upper decks have started to speak. They are not speaking about the cough.

stages.text: The cough count is still on the table where the infirmary left it. The route line waits underneath.

choices.text: Route air to the sick wards.
Refuse. The pressure drop touches everyone.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the worker decks: the people who run the shelter breathe last, since their decks sit farthest from the manifold. The route is drawn. In the margin of her own plan the engineer has written that this is how it should have been built, then signed it; the signature is unlike her.

stages.text: The plan goes around the table. Everybody reads the margin note; everybody reads the signature twice.

choices.text: Leave the manifold as it stands.

quests.briefing: This one is short: fresh oxygen to the children's sector. Lungs that are still growing are being shaped by thin air; the shape is in the infirmary's charts. When the vote is called, the room notices it has already decided. The vote is held anyway, for the record.

stages.text: The vote makes one sound, unanimous. Nobody in the room is surprised by it.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the people no route was ever drawn for: the outcasts, down where the air is twice-recycled. The line is drawn to their door. Someone asks what the outcasts will give in return; the room waits; no answer comes. The asker studies the table.

stages.text: The question of what they will give is still hanging when the vote is called. Nobody repeats it.

choices.text: Refuse. They have managed this long.

quests.briefing: Next are the refugees, the ones who came through the airlock last month: they breathe the thinnest air in the rooms nobody else wanted. The route is drawn and the cost is listed. Someone says they are not ours yet. The room goes quiet; this shelter remembers standing at an airlock once.

stages.text: The words not ours yet stay on the table. The silence they made is still there when the vote is called.

choices.text: Route air to the refugee rooms.

quests.briefing: For once the proposal is practical: fresh oxygen to the surface prep rooms, since the scouts go out breathing thin air and come back to thinner. The route is cheap. The scout lead is asked to speak; she says we would notice, then sits down. That is the entire testimony.

stages.text: The room turns the route plan over in its hands. The scout lead watches them do it.

choices.text: Route air to the prep rooms.
Refuse. Scouts are built for worse.

quests.briefing: The engineer draws the next route herself, to the elder bunks. The margin holds no arithmetic this time, only the names of the people who sleep there. The first name is the man who laid the manifold's first pipe. The room knows its own history when it is shown.

stages.text: The route plan makes the circuit of the table. Everyone who holds it reads the margin to the last name.

choices.text: Route air to the elder bunks.
Refuse. Let them keep the heat instead.

quests.briefing: The proposal is a single line on the manifold's own diagram: equalize all decks; the shelter's air belongs to the shelter. Engineering says it can be done; the cost is that every deck will feel it, which the proposal calls the point. The line has been read aloud twice; nobody heard it right the first time.

stages.text: On the diagram the line crosses every deck at the same height. Nobody asks for a third reading.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is the one nobody wrote, so the engineer wrote it: Command gives up its pure-air loop. The shelter breathes one air or it does not. The council has read it. What the room waits for now is whether anyone on the council will speak first and what they will say.

stages.text: The proposal sits in front of the council. Above their seats the pure-air vent goes on humming at its own pressure.

choices.text: Give up the pure air. All of it.

quests.briefing: Medical supplies are counted in doses now. The Chief Surgeon's first demand is to treat the mildly sick without hesitation; small sicknesses are how big ones start, a lesson the infirmary has learned twice. The demand is written in her own hand; the hand does not shake.

stages.text: The line of the mildly sick runs out the clinic door. She stands at the head of it with the demand in her hand.

quests.briefing: The demand continues: treat the badly injured without hesitation, even when the treatment costs more than the labor. That is where arithmetic stops, she says; the council showed her the arithmetic anyway. She has read it; she has not changed her answer.

stages.text: The arithmetic is still on the table. The room is waiting for an answer she has already given.

choices.text: Refuse. The cost belongs to the shelter.

quests.briefing: Next, the chronic: the people whose treatment never ends, whose doses are counted forever. Treat without hesitation, she says; a shelter that counts its sick is counting something else. She has not said what. The room has heard it anyway.

stages.text: The chronic list is long. She has asked for it to be read in full, so it is read, to the last name.

choices.text: Treat the chronic. All of them.
Refuse. The doses do not stretch forever.

quests.briefing: The demand names the elderly. The council asks what they return; the Chief Surgeon answers with a list of everything they built, two pages, read aloud to the end. The question has not been asked again.

stages.text: The two pages stay on the council table through the vote. Nobody turns them over.

choices.text: Refuse. Winter asks its own questions.

quests.briefing: The demand is hardest this time: treat the terminal without hesitation. The doses will not save them; that is not what the doses are for, she says, out loud. The whole infirmary knew it already. Nobody else had said it.

stages.text: The infirmary is still quiet. The words cannot be unsaid; nobody tries.

quests.briefing: The demand goes outside: the ones taken in from the ash, owed nothing, owing nothing. Treat without hesitation, she says; the clinic door is the one door that does not ask which side of it you were born on. The outsiders were told to wait outside. She has told them to wait inside; the room has let her.

stages.text: The outsiders sit inside now, along the clinic wall. Nobody has told them where else to go.

quests.briefing: The demand crosses the line past the line: treat the enemies without hesitation. Three of them are in the infirmary from the raid; they bleed the same, she says. When the room only looks at her, she says it again, slower. Nobody answers.

stages.text: Three of the raid's wounded lie in the infirmary beds. The vote has not been called yet.

choices.text: Treat them. They bleed the same.
Refuse. They would not treat us.

quests.briefing: This demand is one paragraph; the paragraph has a name in it. The condemned man in the brig is to be treated without hesitation: he is bleeding, the shelter's sentence is the shelter's business, his blood is his. The room divides. The Chief Surgeon takes her kit to the door and waits there with her hand on the latch.

stages.text: The vote is called. The room is not watching the Overseer; it is watching her hand on the latch.

quests.briefing: The demand is arithmetic now; the arithmetic is hers: the last doses go to the lost causes; that, she says, is what the word vow means. She reads the four names aloud; the room knows all four. The vote is not close. It never was.

stages.text: Hands go up. Nobody counts them.

choices.text: Refuse. Four names or forty winters.

quests.briefing: The final demand is a single case: one life, tonight, that will take everything the infirmary has and leave the shelter with nothing tomorrow. The Chief Surgeon does not argue; she says the patient's name, her age, what she asked for this morning. The room does not need to vote. It votes anyway, so the shelter can say it chose.

stages.text: In the infirmary the shelves are counted, dose by dose. Everything on them fits on one tray.

quests.briefing: The brig is full and the laws are harsh; into that, the Overseer has put a proposal the room did not expect: pardon the lazy. Laziness has been a crime here since the first winter; the brig holds eleven people for it. Most of them are grieving; the proposal says so out loud. The room has gone quiet at the word.

stages.text: The list is read aloud in full; no name is skipped. Halfway through the duty officer stops for water; the room waits out the pause.

choices.text: Refuse. The quota is the law.

quests.briefing: Next come the complainers. Raised voices have been logged as offenses here; most of the voices were raised about water. The water was bad; the proposal says so in plain words. While it is read, the water crew stands looking at its hands.

stages.text: On the table by the proposal sits a sealed jar of the old water. Nobody has opened it; nobody needs to.

quests.briefing: The third proposal is for the unlucky: three people sit in the brig for things that broke in their hands, a valve wheel, a pry bar, a gauge face. Everyone in the room has broken something. The proposal asks what the difference is between a hand and a crime, then waits through a long silence. Nobody answers, so the vote is called.

stages.text: The three accused stand at the back with their hands folded. While the list is read, the room looks at its own hands without seeming to notice itself doing it.

quests.briefing: This one is harder: pardon the food thieves. Every theft in the brig is a mouth; every mouth belongs to the shelter. The cook stood up to confirm it; over the years he caught two of them and reported one. The room heard the confession without moving.

stages.text: In the stores ledger, the cook's own initials sit on both incident reports, the filed one and the one that says lost to spoilage.

choices.text: Refuse. Hunger is not a key.

quests.briefing: The proposal moves on to the ones who said no. Some of the orders they refused have since been refused by this entire room; the proposal lists them. The list is read aloud; the room remembers every item on it. The brig holds the people who said it first.

stages.text: Item four on the list draws a sound out of the room before the reader even finishes it. It is not a laugh; nobody looks at anybody.

choices.text: Pardon the ones who said no.

quests.briefing: Now the hoarders; the room bristles: hoarding is the crime this shelter feels in its teeth. The proposal waits for the noise to pass, then reads the list of what was taken and why. The why is mostly children. The bristling does not go away; the vote is called anyway.

stages.text: The items themselves are laid out as evidence: tins, a powdered-milk bag, batteries, one small coat. The coat is what the room keeps looking at.

choices.text: Refuse. The stores belong to the shelter.

quests.briefing: The seventh category is the deserters. The room goes quiet in a way it has not been quiet before; desertion is the crime this shelter fears. The names are read with the posts they walked away from: the north watchtower, the water detail, the surface crew. The room knows every one of those posts; the silence lasts a long time.

stages.text: When the watchtower is named, the duty officer glances toward the man who holds that post now. He stands very straight, as if his shift had already been taken from him.

choices.text: Refuse. The line has to hold.

quests.briefing: The eighth proposal is the one nobody wanted to hear: pardon the violent. Part of the room stood up. The proposal waited it out, then said the word carefully and read the names of those still in the brig for it. Two of the names put people back in their seats; the room watched itself sit down.

stages.text: Five names are on the violent list. The two that settled the room are read last; the reader's voice does not change.

quests.briefing: Last crime: betrayal. The room does not move at all, which is how this room shows fear. There is exactly one betrayal in the brig; the name on it is one this room loved. The proposal makes no argument; it only asks the room to say out loud what it wants done.

stages.text: The name is read once, at normal volume, like any other item. On the wall behind the reader hangs a commendation with the same name on it.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is a single word this shelter has not used since before: amnesty. All of them, every name, every list from the last three months. The Overseer puts the brig key on the council table. The room looks at the key; then it looks at itself.

stages.text: The key is the old mechanical kind, cut for one lock, worn smooth at the grip. From the brig corridor, faintly, comes the sound of people who can hear that the room has gone quiet.

choices.text: Open the brig. All of them.
Refuse. The key stays on the table.

quests.briefing: The injury list is on the table again; the foreman has changed how it is sorted: not by name, by hour. The injuries do not begin in the eighth hour or the ninth. They begin in the eleventh, all of them, as if the body keeps its own ledger. Above the list sits the proposal: eight-hour shifts.

stages.text: The foreman does not argue for it. He lays his left hand on the table beside the list; two fingers of it do not straighten.

quests.briefing: The next ask is the weekend. The quota office says the curve can survive two days of silence; the line crews say nothing. When the oldest worker is called to speak, he stands and says he has forgotten what a Sunday is, then sits down. That is the whole of his testimony.

stages.text: Nobody calls the vote for a long while. In the minutes, the clerk gives his sentence a line of its own.

choices.text: Refuse. The curve does not rest.

quests.briefing: This one is modest: one rest day in seven, for every crew that has not had one since the first winter. Attached is the crew list, in case anyone wants to check who qualifies. It runs to most of the shelter. The room reads it and finds its own names.

stages.text: A few people laugh when they reach their own line. It is not a happy sound, but it settles the vote.

choices.text: Refuse. One day costs one day.

quests.briefing: The fourth ask reaches past the body into the calendar: three holidays a year, named. The names are from before; the clerk reads them in the order the old year kept them. Half the room has not heard them spoken aloud since childhood. Nobody writes them down; nobody needs to.

stages.text: The stillness after the reading lasts a full minute. Then the cook asks which of the three falls first; the room begins, carefully, to plan a meal.

quests.briefing: Sick leave, paid: the fifth ask is the practical one. The shelter already pays for sickness, in fevers that spread down a bunk row and wounds that reopen at the workstation; the infirmary ledger shows it cheaper to rest one worker than to lose six. The medic initials the arithmetic. The vote is not close.

stages.text: The first name on the new roster is a woman who has worked through three fevers. She signs with the medic's pen, then asks what a person does with a day.

choices.text: Refuse. The sick can rest unpaid.

quests.briefing: For months the room has been not-naming what the sixth proposal names: rest owed to the mothers, before and after. The roster knows of four pregnancies; there may be more that it does not. When it is read, the women in the room look at each other. Nobody looks at the men.

stages.text: It is read twice, out of care rather than confusion. It passes faster than anything else the room has voted on.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter cannot afford it.

quests.briefing: Nobody argues with the seventh proposal: bereavement time. The shelter has been burying its dead on the way to the shift, in the hour before the whistle. The proposal asks for three days; the room amends it to five. For the first time, the clerk records no debate at all.

stages.text: The amendment comes from a man whose brother went into the ground in March. He does not explain it; no one asks him to.

choices.text: Refuse. The dead can wait for the living's work.

quests.briefing: The eighth proposal borrows a phrase from the old world: mental health days. The room goes quiet at the luxury of it. Then the proposal reads the infirmary's other list, the one with no wounds on it. The list is long, longer than the injury list was back when injuries were the argument.

stages.text: After the reading, the phrase is not called a luxury again. In the minutes it is entered as medical; the medic says that is only accurate.

quests.briefing: The strangest of the ten asks for art and culture shifts: hours set aside for making things. The room bristles at the word art. Then a woman from the ventilation crew stands and says her daughter has forgotten how to sing. She does not say it as an argument; it ends the argument anyway.

stages.text: The girl is eleven. During the vote she sits on the floor by the door, drawing on the back of a quota sheet.

quests.briefing: The last proposal asks for absolute leisure for the exhausted, which is to say for the shelter itself. One week, paid, no quota; the room amends it to two before the clerk has finished reading. The vote passes without a speech; nobody gets up. Leaving would make it real, so the room sits with it a while longer.

stages.text: On the first morning of the first week, the whistle is not blown. Half the shelter wakes at the usual hour anyway, out of habit.

choices.text: Grant the week. And the second.
Refuse. The shelter runs on the exhausted.

quests.briefing: The mess line has been guessing at the shortfall for weeks; everyone has a figure and none of them match. The proposal on the table is one paragraph: the true food number, read over the PA, once, at dinner. It is typed at the bottom of the page. The typist checked it three times.

stages.text: The number takes four seconds to say. In the mess, nobody's spoon moves during them.

quests.briefing: This time the truth is water. The aquifer report has been in the office drawer for a month; the proposal takes it out and puts two words on the air in the same sentence: aquifer, years. The sentence is eleven words long. It took the clerk an afternoon to write.

stages.text: At the evening count, the sentence goes out once. Cups stop halfway to mouths.

choices.text: Refuse. The word years is too much.

quests.briefing: The filters degrade on a schedule the engineers already keep; the office copy is updated in pencil. The sheet was never marked secret; it was simply never shown. The proposal asks to post it in the mess, where the shelter lines up to eat. The date on it is not far.

stages.text: The sheet goes up beside the menu board. People read it the way they read the menu, then read it again.

quests.briefing: The shelter's heart is slowing; the duty logs have said so for a year, in shrinking margins. This time the proposal is not a number but a person. The engineer has written the truth herself, in her own words. She has asked to read it over the PA; the office has not found a reason to refuse her.

stages.text: She reads standing, one hand flat on the page to still it. At the end she does not editorialize; she switches the microphone off and steps down.

choices.text: Refuse. The heart can slow quietly.

quests.briefing: The broadcast turns inward. The proposal is a list of the office's own errors, read over the PA by the office itself: the miscounted winter, the late seal order, the dry month on the south pump. Before it goes on the air, the list goes around the mess for signatures. It comes back covered in them.

stages.text: Reading it takes eleven minutes. No music plays afterward; the next program is the weather, given in the same flat voice.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs its leaders whole.

quests.briefing: The shelter has been imagining the surface for sixty days; the scouts are the only ones who do not have to imagine. The proposal asks them to say what they saw, over the air, unedited. One scout volunteers. She asks for a night broadcast, when the shifts are in.

stages.text: What she describes first is not the ruins. It is the sky, its color, how long she stood watching it before remembering to be afraid.

quests.briefing: The arithmetic has been done out loud at last: intake against appetite, filters against decay, years against people. It does not end well. There is not a person in the room who has not run a private version of it, on a bunk, in the dark. The proposal is to stop running it privately.

stages.text: The worksheet is read over the PA line by line. The quiet at the end is not surprise; it is recognition.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs the not-knowing.

quests.briefing: The dead have been counted since the first week; the count has never been read aloud. The proposal is to read it over the PA, every name, at walking pace. The list runs to four pages. The clerk who carries it to the booth holds it with both hands.

stages.text: Nobody leaves for the whole of it. When a name lands close to home, nobody turns; the shelter has developed its manners for this.

choices.text: Refuse. The names can stay counted.

quests.briefing: The last number is the end one: how long the shelter has if nothing changes. It has been computed twice, by two people who do not speak to each other; the figures agree. The proposal is to post it by the PA booth and let the shelter look as long as it needs. Both who ran it have asked to initial the posting.

stages.text: The posting goes up on plain paper, no heading. People read it alone, mostly, at different hours, so that no one has to be seen reading it.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is not a fact but a rule. One line, posted beside the PA, voted on once: we say what is true. It is the shortest proposal the room has ever passed. The lowercase ribbon wore out in the winter, so the clerk types it in capitals; nobody asks him to redo it.

stages.text: The first broadcast under the rule is the morning filter report. It is bad news, read plainly, on time.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs its quiet.

quests.briefing: Someone is knocking at the airlock. The camera shows one person, one pack, nothing else on the road in either direction. The knock is steady; the intercom stays silent, as if whoever is out there is saving strength. The cost would be one mouth; the shelter has been asked to vote.

stages.text: Nobody in the room looks at anybody else; they watch the screen. On it, the person sits down in the lee of the door, patient, between knocks.

choices.text: Open the airlock. Take them in.
Keep it shut. We cannot spare the margin.

quests.briefing: There is knocking at the airlock again; this time the camera shows a family: two adults with a child between them. The child is too tired to knock, so the adults take turns. The cost is three mouths. The number sits on the table; nobody says it out loud.

stages.text: On the screen, the child has stopped standing and is being held up between the two adults. One of them keeps knocking; the other keeps wiping dust off the child's face.

choices.text: Keep it shut. Three mouths is three mouths.

quests.briefing: This time the camera shows insignia. The people knocking are scouts from the faction that took from this shelter in the fall; the shelter remembers the fall. They are wounded; they knock with the hand that is not bleeding. The room has been looking at the insignia a long time; at the blood, about as long.

stages.text: One of the scouts has pressed a bandage against the other's side with an elbow, keeping both hands free for knocking. The knock keeps the same slow rhythm.

choices.text: Take them in. Treat the wounds.
Keep it shut. We remember the fall.

quests.briefing: The people at the airlock now are marked: exiles, condemned somewhere else and sent walking. The marks are plain on the camera. Whatever they did, another settlement already judged it; now that judgment stands at the airlock asking to come in. The room has been asked what it believes about borrowed judgments; it has noticed it never asked itself that.

stages.text: The marks are on their forearms, old burns in straight lines, deliberate. On the screen they hold their arms still, as if they know what the camera is for.

choices.text: Take them in. Judge them here.
Keep it shut. Their sentence stands.

quests.briefing: It is not a knock this time, it is a line: an entire rival crew at the airlock, flags down, weapons slung. Their own shelter burned behind them; this one watched the smoke for two days. The cost is not mouths; the cost is rivals, inside. The room looks at the flags; then at the smoke, still on the horizon.

stages.text: Someone has counted them through the scope: nineteen. They stand in column with their own wounded in the middle, drilled as any crew this shelter fields.

choices.text: Open up. Flags down, they come in.
Keep it shut. Rivals stay outside.

quests.briefing: You can hear this knocking through the wall: there is coughing between the knocks. On the camera, cloths are held up for inspection; whoever is out there knows what the shelter will ask. The sickness is legible from here; so is the cost. Asked to speak first, the infirmary said we have beds; it did not say how many.

stages.text: The medic counts them off the screen in a low voice, then stops counting at twelve. The cloths are gray; two of them are dark.

choices.text: Take them in. Quarantine and treat.
Keep it shut. The sickness stays out.

quests.briefing: The knocking is slow now: the dying are at the airlock. Someone told them this shelter buries its dead with names; names are what they came for. They are asking for almost nothing; that is the hard part. The slow knock goes on while the room stays quiet. Nobody calls the vote; nobody wants to be the one who says the word.

stages.text: The burial register is on the shelf behind the council table, a clothbound book with more blank pages than used ones. Someone has already set it on the table, open.

choices.text: Open up. Give them the names.
Keep it shut. We cannot carry more.

quests.briefing: The door dosimeter read this knock before anyone even looked: whoever is out there is hot. The reading is posted by the airlock; the room has read it; everyone here knows what that number means. The people outside know it too. They came anyway; they are still knocking.

stages.text: The posted number is 4.1. Below it, in the duty officer's hand: decon would take the good soap and a day of water.

choices.text: Open up. Straight to the decon line.
Keep it shut. The number is too high.

quests.briefing: It is the knock nobody believed would come: raiders at the airlock, weapons down, hands open, saying the word peace. The word sounds wrong in their mouths; they know it; they have said it again anyway. The settlement they raided is the settlement that would be voting. The room looks at the open hands; then at the names on its own wall.

stages.text: Their weapons are piled ten paces back from the door, where the camera can count them. The one in front keeps his palms turned out, showing empty.

choices.text: Keep it shut. Say the names instead.

quests.briefing: The last vote is not about a knock; it is about a policy: open doors, to all, from now on. A hundred days in, the shelter is deciding what it is; the proposal says it is the place that opens. The cost is posted where the costs always go; the room has read it.
