This vote, the room takes standing.

stages.text: Down the corridor, someone is wiping the dust off the airlock wheel without having been told to. The outer door has not opened since the raiders.

choices.text: Open the doors. All of them.
Keep the doors. Stay what we were.

quests.briefing: The surface has started costing people; the first answer is food. Double rations for scouts. The cook seconded the motion before it was finished being read. The vote went through on the sound of the room, no count taken.

stages.text: The scout table's trays come back double that evening. Nobody at the other tables looks up; the counting was already done out loud.

quests.briefing: Next comes the gear: the best of the protective stock goes to the scouts, who walk into the thing the gear was made for. The inventory readout put the top shelf in command storage, where it had sat since before the first run. The room noticed. The crates came down the same day.

stages.text: The seals on the top-shelf crates had never been cut. The quartermaster cut them himself, logging each piece out by serial number, a whole column of first issues.

quests.briefing: The pay question follows: hazard rates for scouts, drawn in what the shelter has, which is rations, fuel and first pick, posted where everyone can read the numbers. One of the scouts stood at the board a long time and said, not angrily, that it was never about the pay. The room voted the raise through anyway.

stages.text: On the board the numbers sit plain: extra measures, fuel chits, first pick. Under them, in the scouts' own chalk, someone has written the names of the ones who have not come back.

choices.text: Refuse. First pick is too much.

quests.briefing: Then the planning: a run that has gone bad can be aborted; bad is whatever the scout on the ground says it is. The operations office, which draws the maps, has had nothing to say since the motion was read. The vote hands the scouts one new word to carry. The word is no.

stages.text: The maps on the operations table still end where they always ended. Everything past that edge now belongs to one scout's judgment, unappealable.

quests.briefing: Backup comes fifth: armed escorts on every surface run. The surface has started meeting scouts with numbers of its own; the shelter will answer in kind. The armory was asked what it could spare and named it in one short list. The room voted to spend all of it.

stages.text: The backup roster went up within the hour, drawn from the armory's count. The rifles came off the last-line rack; the gaps in the rack are numbered.

choices.text: Refuse. The armory is the last line.

quests.briefing: The sixth measure is the one the scouts have never put on paper: bring the dead home. The surface has been keeping them; the shelter has been letting it. The scout lead carries the cost as a list of names, which she lays on the table. The vote does not need a count.

stages.text: The list stays on the table after the vote, creased soft from being carried. It is older than the room expected; some of the names go back to the first winter.

quests.briefing: The seventh fits in a sentence: scout safety over salvage, always. The rule is to be printed at the top of every order form, above the quota, where it gets read before anything else. The operations office has already set the new forms; the quota now sits second on its own paper.

stages.text: The first run under the new forms goes out in the morning. The officer signing it reads the top line twice before his pen moves, which is what the line is for.

choices.text: Put the rule at the top.

quests.briefing: The eighth is a refusal, written down in advance: the shelter does not draw up suicide missions. The refusal is posted in the room where orders are drawn, so that no one ever has to say no alone again. The scout lead pinned it up herself.

stages.text: It hangs over the drafting table, one line, unsigned. When it was up, the scout lead stood beside it reading a sentence she already knew by heart.

choices.text: Refuse. Some orders must stay possible.

quests.briefing: The ninth nobody else would draft, so the scout lead drafted it herself: the next surface risk belongs to leadership. People who order the risk should know it from the inside. The duty roster lies on the table with the council's names on it. The room is looking at the council.

stages.text: The council has not touched the roster. The quartermaster, who sizes everyone, has brought up gear in their sizes and set it along the wall without being asked.

choices.text: Refuse. The council stays under cover.

quests.briefing: The last is a promise, written out in full: the scouts' protection is absolute. They are the shelter's eyes; the shelter has been spending them. The whole room signs, because a promise should carry every name it can hold. The scouts sign last, since the promise is made to them.

stages.text: The promise hangs now by the surface door, where every run files past it. The scouts' names sit at the bottom in darker ink, added after everyone else had signed.

quests.briefing: The first proposal starts with dignity, priced in water: one day of showers, reserves released. The shelter has been washing with rags out of helmets; it has begun to smell like what it has been through. The quartermaster sets the day's allocation aside without being asked twice. The vote passes in under a minute.

stages.text: The line forms before the water is warm. People come carrying towels folded so long ago that the creases still hold.

quests.briefing: Next the water goes to the clothes. Everything wearable has been worn past wearing; the smell is in the walls now, where the shelter sleeps. A wash day is set, with a laundry list posted by the cistern. The bundles carried down the corridor are heavier than anyone says out loud.

stages.text: Wash day fills the corridor. For two days the shelter drips like a cave; the night shift reports sleeping better for the sound of it.

choices.text: Give the water for the wash.

quests.briefing: The third ask is comfort: warm water, for washing that is not need. The proposal is a single paragraph, most of it one list: hands, faces, whatever else the heart asks. The room reads that line twice. It passes on the first call, without debate.

stages.text: The first evening the warm tap runs, a man shaves for the first time since the exchange. He does not say why; nobody asks.

quests.briefing: This time the water is wanted for colors. The school corner's children have been given paint; paint needs water for mixing. Someone at the table asks what the colors are for; a child answers before the adults can: to make the walls not-walls. The requisition is signed within the hour.

stages.text: A river goes up on the mess-hall wall, blue mixed from the medical dye. By evening there is a queue of children with brushes, each waiting for a section of their own.

choices.text: Give the water for the colors.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the hydroponics bay: flowers, in the middle row, where everyone walks. The food rows flank it; the middle row would be for looking at. Asked whether any seed exists, the bay chief says she has been saving it. That is how the room learns she has been expecting the question for years.

stages.text: She brings the seed down in a spice tin, sorted into folds of paper. Each fold is labeled in pencil with a year.

choices.text: Refuse. The middle row is for calories.

quests.briefing: This one names the animals. The shelter's pets have been drinking out of the ration unofficially; the proposal gives them a line in the ledger. The count is read out: eleven cats, four dogs, a pigeon, something the reactor level insists is a goat. The room laughs; it votes yes before the laughter is done.

stages.text: The goat goes into the ledger as goat, with a question mark. It is the only entry that has one.

choices.text: Refuse. The animals share the ration.

quests.briefing: The quietest of the ten: water for the dying's last requests. The hospice keeps a log of the asking, to wash, to drink, to hold a full cup in both hands. The log is read to the room in full. The vote is a show of hands; every hand is up before the question is finished.

stages.text: The hospice is given its own key to the cistern room. No one has yet asked for it back; no one intends to.

quests.briefing: Now the line itself is the question. The refugees taken in through the airlock have been drinking last since the day they arrived; the proposal moves them to the front. When the quartermaster tells them, they do not believe it. The telling is done again, slower, the ledger open so they can see their names in it.

stages.text: The chalk order on the cistern-room floor is scrubbed out and redrawn the same day. It holds even when no crew member is watching.

quests.briefing: The ninth proposal crosses into something like abundance: a second cup at the evening ration. The board comes down off the mess wall and goes back up with a new figure chalked on it. The settlement studies the figure the way it studies any promise. It holds for a week; the settlement eats.

stages.text: Cups come back for seconds on the first evening of the new figure. People stand at their bunks and drink slowly, to make it last.

choices.text: Raise the ration. Feed them full.
Refuse. Enough is a number we cannot hold.

quests.briefing: The last proposal is the one the shelter has not let itself think: one day of no counting. Every tap open, every cup filled twice, the cistern gauge ignored until morning. The quartermaster schedules the filters around it the way the old world scheduled holidays. It is announced a week ahead; the week passes in disbelief, but the day comes anyway.

stages.text: On the morning of it, a child fills her cup at the mess tap twice running, then looks up to check whether she is allowed. She is.

choices.text: Refuse. Counting is what keeps us alive.

quests.briefing: Someone said in the mess hall that the age of men who decide things alone is over. Somebody else wrote it down, and by that evening it was pinned up by the door with three signatures under it. The first question put to the whole shelter is work hours, and the result is binding. Ballots went round on the backs of ration cards. The count was read out from a crate, and it held, because it belonged to everyone in the room.

stages.text: The count is read out from a crate. It holds. Everyone in the room owns a piece of it.

quests.briefing: The second question is the ration itself, on the argument that a shelter's life should not be set by whoever happens to be holding the ladle. The board went to the floor and came back amended twice: once for the night shift, once for the children. Both amendments are in the minutes. The board went up as amended, and tonight the shelter ate under a rule it wrote.

stages.text: Two amendments off the floor, both logged. The board goes up as amended. The shelter eats under its own rule.

quests.briefing: The third question is the room itself. This shelter has been run by whoever was standing when it needed running; now the standing goes on the ballot. Four people put their names up. The count moved two of them out of the room and one new one into it, and the room let that happen without a hand going anywhere near a door.

stages.text: The count changes who sits in the room. The room lets it. That was the whole of what was being tested.

quests.briefing: Then the law. Everything this shelter punishes people for was read out loud, all of it, and the reading took a full day with two breaks for water. Each rule was voted on separately. Nine were struck out by the floor, including two that somebody in the room had been sentenced under. Nobody left early.

stages.text: The rules are read out one at a time. The ones that fail are struck through in front of everybody. It takes all day, and nobody leaves.

choices.text: Refuse. Justice is not a headcount.

quests.briefing: Now the surface. The shelter spends people up there, so the floor claims the right to say where. The targets went up on the board a day early. The scouts spoke first and at length, because they are the ones who walk them, and one of them said plainly that the north approach would kill somebody. The vote was taken with that still hanging in the room.

stages.text: The scouts speak first; they are the ones who walk it. The settlement votes with what they said still in the air.

quests.briefing: The stores next. The floor wanted the allocation itself rather than a summary of it, then wanted the arithmetic under the allocation, and asked questions for two hours: several of them sharp, one of them about a discrepancy nobody had raised in three years. All of them were answered. The vote passed, and the store doors came open under it.

stages.text: Two hours of questions off the floor, all of them answered, one of them awkward. Then the stores open under the vote.

quests.briefing: Then the outside. Who the shelter stands with decides what the shelter is, so the floor takes that too. The factions were named without euphemism and their terms read out in full, including the clauses nobody enjoyed hearing. One evening settled it, out loud, and everybody walked out of the hall knowing which way it had gone and who had put it there.

stages.text: The terms are read out in full. The settlement votes. The alliance stands or it does not, and nobody has to guess which.

quests.briefing: Then the largest question there is, cut down by the drafting committee to four words on a card: do we stay here. It was read out once, then read out again because the room asked for it. People voted slowly. The answer was read from the same crate as the work-hours count months ago, and the shelter has stood by it since, which is not the same as being at peace with it.

stages.text: Four words on a card: do we stay here. The room asks to hear it twice. Then it votes, slowly, and lives with the answer.

choices.text: Refuse. Fate is not a ballot question.

quests.briefing: The last office to go on the ballot is the highest one. The Overseer was invited to speak in his own defence and took it, for eleven minutes, without notes. Then the floor voted on whether he keeps what he holds. The count was read out in the ordinary way, in an ordinary voice, and the whole room watched him hear it.

stages.text: The floor votes. The count is read out in an ordinary voice. The room watches the Overseer hear it.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is the one every earlier vote was walking toward, and it fits on a single line: one voice, one vote, on everything, permanently. There is no clause for expertise and none for emergencies. An old woman at the back asked about both and was answered honestly, which is that there are none. It passed. The shelter is now precisely the thing it voted to be, and will have to hold a vote about what to do concerning that.

stages.text: One voice, one vote, on everything, permanently. No clause for emergencies. It passes, and the shelter becomes exactly what it chose.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs its structure.
